courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: Being logged in is not a permission. Authentication tells the server *who* is asking; it says nothing about *which* objects and functions that person may touch. Each request needs both answers.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
md: Adding a login in front of an endpoint is not the fix for broken authorization. Peloton's partial fix and USPS's whole design show the result: every registered user, and anyone can register, gets everyone's data.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: DCSync abuses a legitimate protocol: anyone with both replication rights can ask a DC for any password hash. Control who holds those rights, audit 4662 with the replication GUIDs, and treat a DCSync as compromise of every account.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Misconception: "we have CFI, so memory corruption cannot hurt us." CFI guards one rung. An attacker who already has arbitrary read/write can often reach the goal by changing data instead of code pointers (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: EchoLeak: one email, zero clicks, Copilot leaks
md: Every one of Microsoft's controls existed and every one had a gap. Layered defence only works if each layer is complete on its own: all Markdown syntaxes, all allowlisted domains, all retrieval paths.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Misinformation and unbounded consumption
md: Agents multiply consumption: one user request can trigger many model calls and tool calls in a loop. Cap steps per task and total tokens per task, not only per request, or a confused agent (or an injected one) can run until the budget is gone.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: A generator's novelty number is only as good as its reference set and structure matcher. Note that the same disorder issue from the GNoME critique appears here: the synthesized TaCr2O6 was disordered, and MatterGen's ordered-disordered matcher exists so that an ordered variant of a known disordered compound is not counted as new.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
md: An API key in a mobile app or a web page is public. Anyone can unpack the app and read it. Keys that must stay secret belong on servers; a client that runs on the user's device needs a per-user token instead. Defender view: a fixed prefix like `sk_` lets secret scanners find leaked keys in code; log the key id (never the secret) per request and revoke on any leak.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Scopes, consent phishing and refresh token rotation
md: Changing the password does not reliably remove an app's granted consent. RFC 9700 only says servers *may* revoke refresh tokens on a password change, and the consent record itself stays. Response to consent phishing means finding and revoking the app's consent and tokens, not just resetting credentials.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: GraphQL risks: introspection, batching and query depth
md: In GraphQL one request can mean one operation or thousands. Price requests by the work they ask for, check authorization where each field is resolved, and let the server, not the client, decide what is too expensive.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: Source, propagation, sanitiser, sink. A finding is a path from a source to a sink with no sanitiser on it. False positives come from checks the tool cannot understand; false negatives come from sources, sinks or paths it does not model.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
md: KEV says "exploited now", EPSS says "likely soon", CVSS says "how bad if it happens", and your inventory says "where, how exposed, how important". Rank by evidence of exploitation and exposure first, severity second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 1: analysis, then redo that repeats history
md: Redo is decided per page by LSN comparison alone, never by whether the transaction committed. Updates 80 and 100 belong to losers and are redone anyway. After redo the database is exactly as it was at the crash, and only then does undo begin.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Testing input types on your own data
md: Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Inside Tokio's scheduler: local queues, stealing, LIFO slot
md: Tokio guarantees fairness only in a weak sense: if the number of tasks is bounded and no task blocks, every woken task is eventually scheduled. It does **not** promise round-robin order. Two ready tasks A and B may see A scheduled five times before B, even if A calls `yield_now`, a future that returns `Pending` once after arranging its own wakeup, so the scheduler may run something else first.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: Clip length does not map to patches by simple division. YAMNet needs at least 0.975 s of audio (0.96 s plus the rest of the last 25 ms STFT window), pads anything shorter with silence, and rounds longer audio up to a whole hop. Our script gets 1 patch for 0.5 s, **2 patches for 1.0 s**, 10 for 5 s and 20 for 10 s.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
md: Hashing is not encryption. If a company can email you your old password, it is stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted. A hash with no salt is only slightly better than plaintext against an attacker with a list of common passwords.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
md: A TOTP code proves you hold the shared secret right now. It does not prove which website you are typing it into: anyone who sees the code within its 30-second window can use it once. Lesson 12 exploits exactly that gap.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
md: A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI
md: Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
md: Recency alone cannot tell a hot page from a page that was just read once. Every scan-resistant policy adds some second signal: a count, a second reference, or knowledge of which query read the page.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
md: Undefined behavior does not stay on its side of the boundary. The Rust Reference notes that UB in a called C function makes the whole program undefined, including the Rust parts, and vice versa. FFI bindings are where most real-world unsafe Rust lives, so keep them thin and wrap them in a safe API.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
md: Do not hard-code 64 just because it is common. Query the line size: Drepper suggests asking getconf for it at build time and handing it to the compiler as a macro definition (`-DCLS=$(getconf LEVEL1_DCACHE_LINESIZE)`), and if a binary must run everywhere, use the largest line size it may meet.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: DOM-based XSS: when the bug lives in your JavaScript
md: The URL fragment (everything after `#`) is never sent to the server, as MDN's URL guide notes. A DOM XSS that reads `location.hash` leaves no trace in access logs and is invisible to a WAF. It has to be found in the JavaScript itself, by code review, by tests, or by browser-side tools such as DOM Invader, a tool preinstalled as an extension in Burp Suite's built-in browser that tracks sources reaching sinks.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: The contrastive loss on a 4 x 4 batch
md: A common misreading: the off-diagonal pairs are not known to be unrelated. Two captions in a batch may both describe dogs. The loss still pushes them apart, so duplicates and near-duplicates in a batch become false negatives. With 32,768 pairs per batch this is noise the model tolerates, not something the loss detects.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Least privilege, wildcards and the Capital One role
md: `"Resource": "*"` is not always a mistake (a few actions, such as `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, have no narrower resource), but `"Action": "*"` or `"service:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` in an application's role almost always is. Treat each one as a finding that needs a written reason.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: What k-means actually optimises
md: Inertia is the *entire* definition of a good clustering in k-means. Anything you believe about your clusters that inertia does not measure, such as "this point is an outlier" or "this group is a long thin chain", k-means cannot express.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
md: Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Why long tasks fail: compounding errors and verification
md: Task success is roughly a product of step successes, so long tasks need both a high per-step rate and a check after each step that actually detects failure. Check the resulting state, not just whether an action ran.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan only sees code paths that actually run (the manual: it cannot find races in code paths that are not executed). And if, in this particular run, the two threads happened to pass through some unrelated lock in between, that lock creates a happens-before edge and hides the race. Coverage and varied workloads still matter.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: Linearizability is not serializability. Serializability is about transactions over many objects appearing in *some* serial order, with no real-time rule. Linearizability is about single operations on one object, *with* the real-time rule. Their combination is strict serializability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: The balance factor c is a dial between two goods: low c gives tight balance but forwards more requests away from their natural owner (more misses for caches); high c keeps affinity but tolerates more imbalance.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Search guesses; propagation deduces. Every modern CP solver alternates: make one decision, propagate to a fixpoint (repeat until no rule deletes anything more), and backtrack only when some domain becomes empty.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pinning by digest, signing images and verifying at admission
md: Misconception: "a signature means the image is safe". A signature proves who produced it and that it was not changed since. A signed image can still contain vulnerable packages or a backdoor that entered upstream, as in the xz-utils case from the Linux course. Combine signing with scanning and provenance.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
md: AWS states it plainly: "Containers are not a security boundary, and the use of IAM roles for service accounts does not change this." Workload identity scopes credentials per pod, but an escaped container can act as anything on the node. Also, pods with hostNetwork: true always reach IMDS.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
md: Exposed management APIs are the most common real container compromise, and the usual payoff is mining. Every API that can start or exec into containers must require authentication and sit off the internet.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: Misconception: a good standalone rewrite makes state unnecessary. To handle *drop the salary limit*, the rewrite must restate every surviving constraint as text, and the search engine must parse those constraints back into filters. That is two lossy conversions per turn, and a deleted constraint can come back if either one slips.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Ask when the readings are close in probability and a wrong guess is costly or hard to notice. Otherwise, guess the most literal reading, act on it, and make the interpretation visible.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: A clean CoT is not evidence of safety for tasks that do not need a CoT. Chen et al. and Korbak et al. both warn that malign reasoning can happen in activations, so a monitoring-only safety case (an argument that a model is safe to deploy) fails there.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: The cost problem of cross-encoders is not mainly the quadratic attention. It is that the full model, linear layers included, runs for every pair at query time. A bi-encoder pays the same per-token cost too, but for the documents only once, offline.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
md: A block cipher on its own encrypts exactly one block. Real messages are many blocks, and how you chain them (the **mode**) decides whether patterns leak. Calling raw AES block by block is the mistake of the next lesson.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
md: Every level of the hierarchy does the same thing: stage a tile in a faster, smaller memory and reuse it across as many math operations as the capacity of that memory allows. Tile shapes are the main tuning knobs of a CUTLASS GEMM.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: Fast CUTLASS kernels come from a few choices: tile shape (reuse versus occupancy and wave fit), stage count (latency hiding versus shared memory), kernel schedule (cooperative or ping-pong) and the epilogue fusion. CuTe layouts make each choice a type parameter instead of a rewrite.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Placing pages: tiering in Linux, pooling in Pond
md: CXL makes memory placement a policy problem again. The hardware gives you a slower, bigger NUMA tier; the operating system (tiering) or the cluster manager (pooling) must keep hot data local and push only cold or untouched data to it.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
md: Measure what the hot path *reads repeatedly*. Splitting the search key from its payload shrinks the working set the loop revisits, which often matters more than the miss count of a single call.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Reviewing infrastructure as code: reading a Terraform plan
md: The most dangerous line in a plan is often not an open port but a `-/+` or `-` on something stateful: a database, a bucket, a KMS key. Replacements are triggered by innocent-looking edits (a renamed resource, a changed engine version), and a reviewer skimming for security groups will miss them.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Do not read 'parallel generation' as 'all tokens in one step'. Quality drops quickly when many interdependent tokens are committed together; useful systems unmask a few to a few dozen tokens per pass depending on confidence.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Chunked prefill bounds interference inside one GPU; disaggregation removes it and lets each phase get its own hardware, parallelism and scale. Pick by measuring per-GPU goodput under your SLOs, prompt lengths and interconnect, not by architecture preference.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
md: Do not read DPO's $\beta$ as a guarantee of staying close to the reference. On pairs the model already separates, DPO's gradient shrinks but never pushes back, so drift continues as long as you keep training. The IPO paper notes that early stopping is the usual extra guard.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
md: A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
md: Probe context matters. `tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue` often fires in the context of the process that issued the I/O, but it can also fire from kernel context (for example readahead, where the kernel reads file pages before anyone asks for them), so `comm` and `pid` may not name the application you expect.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Overthinking: 901 tokens to say 2 + 3 = 5
md: Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: One meter, many appliances: the disaggregation problem
md: Real aggregates are not the clean sum of the appliances you know about. UK-DALE reports that in House 1, with monitors on almost every appliance, only 80% of the energy was sub-metered, partly because the 52 plug monitors themselves draw about 50 W. The $\varepsilon_t$ term is never zero.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
md: Stripping is lossy. NFKC turns the superscript in `i⁹` into a plain `9`, and a stopword list (words deleted from every key because they seem uninformative) that drops `group`, `bank` or `the` can merge different companies. Strip only tokens that never distinguish entities in your data, apply cleaning to the matching key, and keep the original string.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: Readiness is a hint, not a promise. The [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html) page warns that a socket can be reported readable and a following read can still block, for example when the arrived packet had a bad checksum and was dropped. That is why event loops always use nonblocking sockets.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
md: Hold out queries, not pairs, and cluster near-duplicates before splitting. Tune on dev as much as you like, read the sealed test set rarely and for decisions you declared in advance, and replace it on a schedule.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
md: NX turns "write code, then run it" into "write data, then crash". It does not stop the hijack of the return address; it removes the attacker's easiest thing to jump *to*.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Why a write steals the whole line: MESI and ownership
md: False sharing needs three things at once: two or more cores, one cache line, and at least one writer. Remove any one (single thread, separate lines, or read-only data) and the line stops bouncing.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
md: A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
md: Finer is not free forever. Each expert becomes a smaller matrix multiply, which gives the GPU less work per launch to spread over its many parallel cores, so it runs less efficiently. DeepSeekMoE 16B stopped at experts one quarter the size of a standard FFN, citing the potential loss of computational efficiency from excessively small experts. DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed experts with an intermediate width of 2048.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: The page table is a block-sparse matrix
md: Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
md: A primed equation is not an assignment; an action is a true-or-false formula about a pair of states. If an action says nothing about a variable, the next value is unconstrained. TLC refuses such a spec: dropping `UNCHANGED tmp` from Write makes it stop with "Successor state is not completely specified by action Write".

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
md: Not every tensor tolerates coarse grouping. DeepSeek tried quantizing activation gradients in 128x128 blocks (so only a transpose would be needed in the backward pass). A 16B MoE model trained for about 300B tokens diverged: Dgrad feeds every earlier layer in a chain and is very precision-sensitive. Activation gradients keep fine 1x128 tiles.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
md: After fsync fails on buffered data, assume the dirty data is gone. Do not retry and continue: recover from a log you know is durable. That is why PostgreSQL's [data_sync_retry](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-error-handling.html) defaults to off, which turns such a failure into a PANIC and a WAL replay.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: To compare two fuzzing setups: 30 or more runs each, at least 24 hours, the same documented seeds, a statistical test, and bugs counted by distinct fixes. Anything less is an anecdote.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Publishing a working exploit is a separate, debated decision (OWASP notes both sides). It is never needed to get a memory-safety bug fixed: the sanitizer report and minimised input are proof. This course's path ends at the fix and the advisory.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess
md: Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Misconception: latitude and longitude are x and y on a flat grid. They are angles on a sphere. Any shortcut that treats them as planar (Euclidean distance on degrees, fixed-size degree boxes) is wrong by a factor of $1/\cos\varphi$ in the east-west direction and breaks at 180 degrees longitude and near the poles.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Convolution: separable passes and the shared-memory halo
md: Tiling turns $k^2$ loads per output into roughly 1 plus halo, and the halo shrinks as the tile gets wider. Separability turns $k^2$ multiply-adds into $2k$ but adds a full intermediate write and read. Large windows want both; small windows on byte data often want tiling alone.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Reusing a freed block on the same stream is safe without synchronization because stream order already serializes the old and new users. Cross-stream reuse needs events: record_stream in PyTorch, event dependencies in cudaMallocAsync pools.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: **Padding by any amount does not work.** The conflict degree is $\gcd(\text{row width}, 32)$. A row width of 33 gives 1, but a width of 34 gives a 2-way conflict and 48 gives 16-way. Pick an odd width.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Low occupancy always costs you latency hiding; high occupancy does not always buy you speed. Use the `launch__occupancy_limit_*` metrics to learn which resource caps you, then decide whether that cap is actually the thing hurting the kernel.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch
md: Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: The headline result is GraphRAG versus vector RAG on global sensemaking questions: 72 to 83% comprehensiveness win rates on Podcast. Against map-reduce over raw text, the advantage is small; the bigger win there is token cost at query time.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Power, EM, sound and faults: physical side channels
md: Physical side channels need the attacker close to the device, but that is exactly the threat model of smart cards, phones, payment terminals, hardware wallets and secure enclaves. Hertzbleed shows the line between physical and remote is not fixed: when power controls frequency, power becomes timing.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: What OT and ICS are, and why they are not just IT
md: A common mistake is to treat a plant like an office network: run an aggressive vulnerability scan, push patches overnight, reboot to clean an infection. NIST warns that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT 'may cause availability and timing disruptions'. In OT the security team works with control engineers, not around them.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
md: Three layers stood between the change and an overflow: humans watching the HMI (defeated by the replay), network monitoring (raised an alert at minute 10), and an independent safety system with its own sensor (tripped at minute 26). Design so that the last layer does not share any path with the first two.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
md: Frameworks tell you what good looks like (62443, NIST), what is mandatory in your sector (NERC CIP for the bulk grid), and how attackers behave (ATT&CK for ICS). Use all three, but remember the cases: most real compromises came through remote access, default passwords and flat networks.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Events, alerts and incidents: when does it become an incident?
md: An incident starts when the attacker acts, not when you declare it. The HSE intrusion began on 18 March 2021 and was declared on 14 May. The gap (dwell time) is what your logs, memory and timeline work must reach back across.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Acquisition: memory, disk images, cloud snapshots and logs
md: Encryption changes the plan. If a disk uses BitLocker or another full-disk encryption, an image taken after power-off is unreadable without the recovery key. Capture what you need from the running system, or make sure the key is in your hands before you shut it down.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Blameless postmortems, lessons learned and tabletop exercises
md: Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable. It means the review asks why the system let a reasonable person make that choice, and fixes the system: alert routing, ownership, tooling, training.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle is sound but not complete: everything it reports is real, but it can miss anomalies. A cycle found is real, yet missing cycles prove nothing: appends never observed by a later read leave gaps in the version order, and predicate anomalies (like phantoms, rows matching a WHERE clause that appear or vanish between two reads in one transaction) are outside its analysis.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Misconception: bypass is mainly about avoiding copies. The kernel already offers zero-copy paths. At 14.88 Mpps the killers are fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, mode switches, metadata setup, shared locks), which is why minimum-size packets are the benchmark that matters.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Counting bytes: the chain before and after fusion
md: Fused bytes = what you must read + what you must keep. Everything in between is the saving. For a chain of k unary elementwise ops on the same tensor with no side outputs, eager moves about k times the fused bytes.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
md: A more accurate teacher is not automatically a better teacher, and a student that improves is not necessarily copying its teacher. Measure student accuracy directly; try a smaller or early-stopped teacher, or a teacher assistant, when the gap is large.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
md: Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
md: Lamport clocks do not detect concurrency. From $L(a) < L(b)$ you may conclude only that b did not happen before a. Any code that treats a larger Lamport timestamp as "definitely caused by" is wrong.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
md: Cheap approximate scores filter, exact scores decide. PLAID is the same funnel as BM25 followed by a cross-encoder, built inside one model: centroid ids are the cheap representation and decompressed vectors are the precise one.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Always handle the case where the search lands on the edge of the window. With stored min/max bounds, a hit on the boundary is the signal that a non-monotonic model may have pushed the true answer outside.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly. The coming lessons build each of these.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
md: The state is a key-value memory with room for about $d_k$ clean associations per head. Linear attention writes to it with a purely additive rule, so it can neither correct an old association nor make room for new ones.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
md: Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Defense in depth: input, prompt, output and grounding layers
md: Masking the model's input and output does not mask everything else. The AWS docs say Bedrock invocation logs (its record of each model call) keep the original request, and the `match` field of the guardrail trace (the per-request report of what each policy found) contains the original PII value by design. Protect logs and traces separately.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
md: The constraint and the prompt are separate channels. A mask can stop the model from writing an illegal token, but it cannot tell the model what the fields mean. If the model never sees the schema (as with llama.cpp's grammar option), describe the fields in the prompt, or the model is forced through a format it does not understand.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
md: Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris scores a window by how much it changes under shifts in every direction. Both eigenvalues of $M$ large means corner; that is what makes a point localizable in two dimensions.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Why log at all, and why not log everything
md: The log you need is usually older than the moment you learn you need it. Decide what to collect and how long to keep it from the questions an investigation will ask, then pay for that deliberately.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Alert quality: precision, recall and the base-rate trap
md: Low precision does not just waste time; it trains people to ignore alerts. Target's alerts were real, but an alert stream that is usually wrong teaches analysts that the next one probably is too. Precision is a security property.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
md: Malware can notice it is in a VM and change behaviour (ATT&CK calls this Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, T1497). An empty or 'boring' run does not prove a file is benign; it may prove only that the sample saw your lab.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: C2 detection rests on things the operator finds hard to change: timing patterns, the process making the connection, rare destinations, and on-host artifacts. Fortra's own guide shows the traffic shape can be reconfigured (Malleable C2 profiles let an operator change how Beacon's HTTP traffic looks), so content signatures alone age quickly.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why Matryoshka prefixes are safe for shortlisting.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: Removing a node and freeing it are different events. Every scheme in this course defers the free until no thread can still hold a reference taken before the removal.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: What memory safety means and why breaking it is dangerous
md: C and C++ do not check bounds or lifetimes for you. Every array index, every length and every `free` is a promise the programmer must keep by hand. Memory safety bugs are what happens when one promise is broken, and the attacker gets to choose the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Uninitialized memory and type confusion
md: Uninitialized reads leak what came before; type confusion reinterprets what is there. Both are fixed the same way in spirit: never let code read bytes whose meaning it has not established, by initializing first and checking tags before use.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache, storing each element in fewer bits such as FP8 (an 8-bit floating-point format) or lower, is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: Returning from FUTEX_WAIT does not mean the lock is yours. The call can fail with EAGAIN, be interrupted by a signal (EINTR), or wake spuriously (return as if woken although no wake was meant for this lock), and another thread may grab the lock first. Always loop and re-check the word.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed: new snapshot per statement, writers re-apply on top of concurrent commits. Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction, writers that hit a concurrent commit get error 40001 and must retry.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
md: Never report token accuracy for NER. CoNLL-2003 English training data holds one entity per 8.7 tokens, so the great majority of tags are O and a tagger that predicts O everywhere scores high token accuracy with an entity F1 of exactly zero. Entity-level micro F1 is the metric; token accuracy is a training diagnostic at best.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
md: Training parallelism and generation parallelism are separate settings. For example vLLM's `tensor_parallel_size` is unrelated to Megatron's `tensor_model_parallel_size`. Refit must reshape weights from the trainer's layout into the engine's layout, which is part of why refit transports matter (lesson 4).

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: SYN floods and SYN cookies
md: A SYN flood attacks memory, not bandwidth: a few packets per second can hold a backlog full. SYN cookies move the half-open state into the sequence number the client must echo, so spoofed SYNs cost the server almost nothing.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
md: A MAC address is not an identity. Operating systems let you change it, [Android](https://source.android.com/docs/core/connect/wifi-mac-randomization) uses a randomized address per Wi-Fi network by default since Android 10, and it never leaves the local link: routers replace it at every hop. "Allow only these MAC addresses" stops honest mistakes, not attackers.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
md: Captures contain other people's data: passwords, messages, cookies. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, keep the files protected, and delete them when done. Intercepting others' traffic without authorisation is illegal in most countries (the security basics course covers the law).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: NMS is not learned and does not look at the image. It only sees boxes and scores. It cannot remove a confident false positive that overlaps nothing (B3), and in dense scenes it removes real objects that happen to overlap.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation
md: A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
md: MAC limits damage; it does not remove bugs. The SELinux Notebook is blunt: SELinux "will not stop memory leaks or buffer over-runs" and "will not stop kernel vulnerabilities", though it may contain their effects. A policy also cannot stop anything it allows.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Putting it together: one service, many layers
md: Assume each layer will fail and ask what the next one still guarantees: least privilege inside the program (privsep, drops), MAC around it, seccomp and capabilities on its kernel access, namespaces and cgroups around its view, and a separate kernel when the code is hostile. Patching is the layer under all of them.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: CI is a contract written in the repo: on these events, on these machines, run these commands, and block the merge unless they exit with status 0. Read `.github/workflows/` before your first PR to a project.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Misconception: a reviewer who leaves 15 comments is blocking you on all 15. Often most are optional. If the reviewer did not say which ones block the merge, ask instead of guessing.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: Read in this order before you touch code: LICENSE (can you contribute at all), CONTRIBUTING (how), CODE_OF_CONDUCT (how to behave), SECURITY (if your finding is a vulnerability). Ten minutes of reading avoids a rejected PR.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebase rewrites history. The rule from Pro Git, the free Git book on git-scm.com: do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on. Your own PR branch is the usual exception, which is why the next lesson's force-push needs care, not a ban.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: Public is not the same as open source. Code you can read on GitHub with no license file is all rights reserved, and so is a snippet whose license you never checked.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: CLA: one signed agreement per person or company, granting rights up front. DCO: no agreement, just a per-commit certification of origin via Signed-off-by, checked mechanically by email match.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
md: A common mistake is to fix a bug inside a generated file. Your edit is overwritten the next time the generator runs, and reviewers will reject it. When a file says *do not edit*, find its input (here `src/commands/get.json`) in the build rule and change that instead.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: Every cut is an experiment: remove, rerun, compare to the original failure. Keep cuts that preserve the exact error; undo the rest.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: If the project squash-merges PRs, your intermediate commits disappear from the main branch anyway, and the PR as a whole becomes one commit. That makes **one logical change per PR** even more important: the squash cannot separate a fix from a speedup after the fact.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
md: Ambiguity is what got two professionals arrested. Write down: who owns each target, who signed for it, when testing may happen, who outside the client has been told, and two 24/7 ways to reach someone who can confirm it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
md: A sampling profiler answers one question: what fraction of CPU samples had this function on the stack? It is cheap because work happens per sample, not per call, and it is approximate because it is a sample.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Common misconception: "unflushed stores are lost on a crash." Some are, some are not, and the hardware chooses. Treat each dirty cache line as independently maybe-persisted. Flushes give you a lower bound on what is durable, never an upper bound.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
md: Authentication checks answer "was this domain's use authorised?", never "is this message honest?". A display-name spoof or lookalike domain passes them cleanly. Defences need both: DMARC against exact-domain spoofing, and human-facing cues plus process rules for the rest.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
md: Two rules give every struct layout: **each field's offset is a multiple of its alignment**, and **the struct's size is a multiple of its own alignment** (the largest field alignment). Everything else, including all the padding, follows from these.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Real-time tracking, 3D lifting and joint angles for apps
md: Keypoints are noisy, especially when occluded. Before writing rules on them: check per-keypoint visibility or score, prefer 3D world landmarks or a side view for sagittal angles (bends in the side-view plane that splits the body into left and right) such as the knee, smooth over a few frames, and use two thresholds (hysteresis) rather than one.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
md: Common misconception: "faster RAM will speed up my tree or hash-chain lookups." Faster transfer rates raise peak bandwidth, but a dependent chain of misses uses a tiny fraction of it. Its cost is set by latency, which has improved far more slowly.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
md: Misconception: "we have MFA, so stolen hashes and tickets don't matter." Multi-factor authentication protects the sign-in that asks for it, usually remote access and cloud portals. Inside a Windows network, NTLM and Kerberos authentication to a file server or another workstation uses the hash or ticket directly and does not prompt for a second factor.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: PRMs give denser, more precise feedback than outcome checks, but they are learned models: they can be exploited by search and RL, they degrade under distribution shift, and their labels (human, MC, or judge) each carry their own noise. Use them where search or reranking pays off and keep the final-answer verifier in the loop.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Training per-slice codebooks and encoding a vector
md: Common misconception: a PQ code is a lossless compression of the vector. It is not. Two different vectors with the same code are indistinguishable to the index, and every distance computed from codes inherits the quantization error.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
md:
Two separate objects, and you must keep them apart:

- **sequence**: which of the 20 amino acids sits at each position (discrete, one symbol per residue)
- **backbone**: where the N, CA, C and O atoms of every residue sit in 3D space (continuous coordinates)

The chain folds into one preferred backbone shape, and that shape is what gives the protein its function.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Never write a bare `except:` or `except Exception: pass` around a whole script. It also swallows bugs in your own code and even Ctrl+C in the bare form, so the script reports "no alerts" when it actually crashed on line 2. Catch the specific exception you expect, at the place you can handle it, and let everything else fail loudly.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Enriching indicators: threat-intel lookups within rate limits
md: Every enrichment client needs the same five parts: strict input validation, a timeout, explicit handling of 404 and 429, a pace that respects the documented limit, and a cache so duplicates are free.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
md: The retriever only sees what you send it. Rewriting changes *which* query is sent; decomposition changes *how many* queries are sent and in what order. Both are bets that a better query beats a better index.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
md: Unbiased does not mean accurate on each pair. It means the errors average out to zero instead of pushing every estimate the same way. Per-pair accuracy comes from concentration: the 1/sqrt(D) shrinkage.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
md: Filling a missing value with 0 is safe only when 0 already means the worst value. For a feature like 1/window it does. For a z-scored feature, 0 means average, so a missing value silently becomes an average document. Use the worst observed value (LETOR's MIN approach) or add a separate is-missing flag.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
md: RDMA is not "the OS is gone". The kernel driver still creates queues, pins and maps memory, and handles errors. What disappears is per-message kernel work. That split between a slow **control path** and a fast **data path** is the design of the whole API.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: The authoritative server and its fixed tick
md: An authoritative server makes the server state the only truth. Every latency trick in the next lessons changes only what the *client displays*; none of them lets a client decide the outcome.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Do not drop the zeros. Training only on observed implicit events (all with p = 1) lets the model predict 1 everywhere and still reach zero loss. The low-confidence zeros are what make the scores discriminative.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why one pixels-per-mm ratio fails on a tilted photo
md: A common misconception is that the pixels-per-mm method only fails at extreme angles. In this toy, a moderate 40 degree tilt already puts it 15 percent off. Under perspective, scale varies with both position and direction across the plane.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The planner is only as good as its row estimates. It searches join orders exhaustively by dynamic programming up to a limit, then genetically; but a 100x row misestimate can turn the cheapest-looking plan into the slowest. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE estimates against actuals first.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
md: Unhackability is a very strong condition. For rich policy classes, every proxy that is not simply equivalent to the true reward (same ranking of all policies) can be hacked by some policy. Skalse et al. conclude that learned rewards are better treated as aids to policy learning than as specifications to optimize without limit. The practical question becomes how far you can optimize before hacking appears.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Assessing risk in practice: from asset list to risk register
md: An auditor asking about risk management wants to see: a documented method (scales, appetite), a register with named owners, dated decisions by people with the authority to make them, and evidence that the register is reviewed on schedule. A register nobody reviews fails the audit even if every score is right.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: NIST CSF 2.0: six functions, profiles and tiers
md: CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; 22 categories, 106 subcategories; current and target profiles define your roadmap; tiers describe rigour. Voluntary, outcome-based and free, which makes it the common language between engineers, executives and other frameworks.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
md: Notification duties stack. One ransomware incident at a cloud provider in Germany can mean a GDPR notification to the data protection authority (72 hours), a NIS2 early warning to the CSIRT (24 hours), DORA reports via financial customers, and contractual notices to customers. Decide in advance who files which report; the clocks start whether or not you have a plan.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Accountability: what boards, CISOs and engineers have answered for
md: Red flags that should make any engineer escalate in writing: being asked to delete or delay logs, to describe an intrusion as "research", to pay an attacker through a bug bounty, to tell a regulator or customer something you know is false, or to keep the general counsel or board out of the loop. Follow your company's whistleblowing or escalation path; your own integrity is the control.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
md: Staleness is a dial, not a free lunch. Too tight a bound and the system stalls behind long trajectories again (AReaL notes small eta slows generation and recommends a large one); too loose and updates use data from much older policies, which prior work shows can degrade learning. Importance weights can also explode for tokens the behavior policy found unlikely, which is why verl truncates or rejects extreme ratios.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: MTTR: detect, triage, mitigate, resolve
md: Mitigating destroys evidence. Reverting the config drains the queue, restarts pods and rotates the logs that held the smoking gun. Before you revert, spend the 30 seconds: snapshot the pool metrics, grab one stack dump, copy the rendered config, note the exact timestamps. The chapter's phrase is that rapid triage does not preclude preserving evidence of what is going wrong.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Weighted RRF and multi-query fusion (RAG-Fusion)
md: Multi-query fusion has costs. In the Infineon study RAG-Fusion averaged 34.62 s versus 19.52 s for plain RAG (1.77 times slower in that deployment), mostly from the larger answer call, and some answers strayed off topic when the generated queries were not relevant enough. If the rewrites are near-duplicates, fusion just re-counts the same list.
